front: What does "at-most-once" delivery mean for a message?
back: Each message is delivered zero or one times; it may be lost but is never processed more than once.
accepted_answers: Each message is delivered zero or one times; it may be lost but is never processed more than once.
hint: The risk is loss, not duplication.

front: What does "at-least-once" delivery mean for a message?
back: Each message is delivered one or more times; it is never silently lost, but a consumer may see it more than once.
accepted_answers: Each message is delivered one or more times; it is never silently lost, but a consumer may see it more than once.
hint: The risk is duplication, not loss.

front: Why is "exactly-once" delivery across two independent systems (for example, Kafka to an external payment API) generally not achievable as a hard guarantee?
back: There is no way for the sender to atomically know the receiver both processed the message and will never see a duplicate, since acknowledgments themselves can be lost or delayed; the practical answer is at-least-once delivery paired with an idempotent receiver.
accepted_answers: There is no way for the sender to atomically know the receiver both processed the message and will never see a duplicate, since acknowledgments themselves can be lost or delayed; the practical answer is at-least-once delivery paired with an idempotent receiver.
hint: The guarantee has to move from the transport to the receiver's own idempotency.

front: A Kafka producer sets acks=0. What delivery risk does this configuration accept?
back: The producer does not wait for any broker acknowledgment, so messages can be silently lost if the broker never receives or persists them, in exchange for the lowest latency.
accepted_answers: The producer does not wait for any broker acknowledgment, so messages can be silently lost if the broker never receives or persists them, in exchange for the lowest latency.
hint: Fire-and-forget: fastest, least safe.

front: What does acks=all (or acks=-1) require before a Kafka producer considers a write successful?
back: Acknowledgment from all in-sync replicas (not just the partition leader), so the write is durable even if the current leader immediately fails.
accepted_answers: Acknowledgment from all in-sync replicas (not just the partition leader), so the write is durable even if the current leader immediately fails.
hint: Wait for the full in-sync replica set, not just one broker.

front: What does enabling the idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) prevent?
back: Duplicate messages caused by the producer's own retries, by having the broker deduplicate retried sends from the same producer session using sequence numbers, without changing the number of times the application called send.
accepted_answers: Duplicate messages caused by the producer's own retries, by having the broker deduplicate retried sends from the same producer session using sequence numbers, without changing the number of times the application called send.
hint: It removes duplicates introduced purely by network-level retry, not application-level retries.

front: What does a Kafka transactional producer add on top of the idempotent producer?
back: The ability to write to multiple partitions/topics (and commit consumer offsets) as a single atomic unit, so a consume-transform-produce pipeline can achieve exactly-once semantics within Kafka.
accepted_answers: The ability to write to multiple partitions/topics (and commit consumer offsets) as a single atomic unit, so a consume-transform-produce pipeline can achieve exactly-once semantics within Kafka.
hint: It extends per-message idempotence into an atomic multi-write transaction.

front: Why is Kafka's transactional exactly-once guarantee scoped to "Kafka-to-Kafka" rather than the whole pipeline?
back: The atomic commit only covers writes and offset commits within Kafka itself; once a consumer's output leaves Kafka (a database write, an external API call), that external side effect is not covered by the same transaction and can still be duplicated or lost.
accepted_answers: The atomic commit only covers writes and offset commits within Kafka itself; once a consumer's output leaves Kafka (a database write, an external API call), that external side effect is not covered by the same transaction and can still be duplicated or lost.
hint: The transaction boundary stops at Kafka's own log.

front: A consumer commits its offset immediately after polling a batch, before processing the messages. What failure mode does this create?
back: If the consumer crashes while processing, the offset is already committed, so those messages are skipped on restart and effectively lost, even though they were never actually handled.
accepted_answers: If the consumer crashes while processing, the offset is already committed, so those messages are skipped on restart and effectively lost, even though they were never actually handled.
hint: Committing before doing the work risks losing the work.

front: A consumer processes each message and commits its offset only after successful processing. Under a crash mid-batch, what does the consumer see on restart, and what must it therefore tolerate?
back: It will reprocess messages from the last committed offset onward, including some it already handled before the crash, so the consumer must be idempotent to stay correct under at-least-once redelivery.
accepted_answers: It will reprocess messages from the last committed offset onward, including some it already handled before the crash, so the consumer must be idempotent to stay correct under at-least-once redelivery.
hint: Commit-after-processing trades "never lost" for "sometimes duplicated."

front: Within a single Kafka partition, what ordering guarantee does Kafka provide?
back: Messages within one partition are delivered to a consumer in the exact order they were appended (their offset order); Kafka does not guarantee ordering across different partitions.
accepted_answers: Messages within one partition are delivered to a consumer in the exact order they were appended (their offset order); Kafka does not guarantee ordering across different partitions.
hint: Order is a per-partition guarantee, not a per-topic one.

front: An event stream needs all events for the same customer processed in order, but the topic has many partitions for throughput. How should the producer choose a partition key to satisfy both requirements?
back: Use the customer ID as the partition key so every event for that customer hashes to the same partition, preserving per-customer order, while different customers spread across partitions for parallelism.
accepted_answers: Use the customer ID as the partition key so every event for that customer hashes to the same partition, preserving per-customer order, while different customers spread across partitions for parallelism.
hint: Same key, same partition, is how you buy ordering without giving up parallelism.

front: During a Kafka consumer group rebalance, why can a message be processed twice even by a well-behaved idempotent-producer setup?
back: Partitions get reassigned between consumer instances, and if the previous owner had processed messages but not yet committed its offset before losing the partition, the new owner starts from the last committed offset and reprocesses them.
accepted_answers: Partitions get reassigned between consumer instances, and if the previous owner had processed messages but not yet committed its offset before losing the partition, the new owner starts from the last committed offset and reprocesses them.
hint: Rebalances can hand off a partition mid-flight relative to the old owner's uncommitted progress.

front: What is consumer lag?
back: The difference between the latest offset produced to a partition and the offset a consumer group has last committed, representing how far behind the consumer is from real-time.
accepted_answers: The difference between the latest offset produced to a partition and the offset a consumer group has last committed, representing how far behind the consumer is from real-time.
hint: It measures how many unread messages are waiting for the consumer.

front: Consumer lag on one topic keeps growing steadily during business hours even though the service is not crashing. What two broad causes should an on-call engineer investigate first?
back: Either the consumer is processing too slowly relative to the incoming message rate (needs more consumers/partitions or faster processing), or a downstream dependency the consumer calls per message is slow or throttling, stalling the whole poll loop.
accepted_answers: Either the consumer is processing too slowly relative to the incoming message rate (needs more consumers/partitions or faster processing), or a downstream dependency the consumer calls per message is slow or throttling, stalling the whole poll loop.
hint: Growing lag is a throughput problem: too much in, not enough processed out.

front: What is the in-sync replica (ISR) set for a Kafka partition?
back: The set of replicas, including the leader, that are fully caught up with the leader's log and are eligible to be elected leader without data loss.
accepted_answers: The set of replicas, including the leader, that are fully caught up with the leader's log and are eligible to be elected leader without data loss.
hint: Only replicas that are current enough to safely take over belong to this set.

front: What risk does enabling "unclean leader election" introduce?
back: A replica that is not fully caught up (not in the ISR) can be elected leader to keep the partition available, which can silently lose the most recently acknowledged messages that never replicated to it.
accepted_answers: A replica that is not fully caught up (not in the ISR) can be elected leader to keep the partition available, which can silently lose the most recently acknowledged messages that never replicated to it.
hint: It trades durability for availability during an outage.

front: What does min.insync.replicas=2 combined with acks=all guarantee together for a topic with replication factor 3?
back: A write is only acknowledged once at least two replicas (including the leader) have it, so the topic tolerates one broker failure without any acknowledged write being lost.
accepted_answers: A write is only acknowledged once at least two replicas (including the leader) have it, so the topic tolerates one broker failure without any acknowledged write being lost.
hint: Durability comes from requiring more than just the leader to have the data.

front: What is the "dual-write problem" when a service updates its own database and then separately publishes an event to Kafka?
back: The database write and the Kafka publish are two independent operations with no shared transaction, so a crash between them can leave the database updated with no event published, or an event published with no matching database change.
accepted_answers: The database write and the Kafka publish are two independent operations with no shared transaction, so a crash between them can leave the database updated with no event published, or an event published with no matching database change.
hint: Two systems, one intent, no atomic boundary spanning both.

front: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
back: Write the business change and a corresponding event row to an "outbox" table in the same local database transaction, then have a separate relay process read the outbox table and publish those events to Kafka, deleting or marking them once published.
accepted_answers: Write the business change and a corresponding event row to an "outbox" table in the same local database transaction, then have a separate relay process read the outbox table and publish those events to Kafka, deleting or marking them once published.
hint: Make the event part of the same local transaction as the business change; publish it out-of-band afterward.

front: Why does the outbox pattern solve the dual-write problem even though the Kafka publish still happens as a separate step afterward?
back: The business change and the fact that "an event needs to be published" are committed atomically in one local transaction; the relay's job is just to guarantee that recorded outbox row is eventually published at least once, which is a simpler, retryable problem than atomically writing to two different systems.
accepted_answers: The business change and the fact that "an event needs to be published" are committed atomically in one local transaction; the relay's job is just to guarantee that recorded outbox row is eventually published at least once, which is a simpler, retryable problem than atomically writing to two different systems.
hint: Atomicity moves to the single database transaction; publishing becomes an at-least-once retry loop.

front: What is change data capture (CDC), and how is it used as an alternative outbox relay?
back: CDC tools (such as Debezium) read a database's transaction/replication log directly and stream row changes as events, which can publish outbox table inserts to Kafka without the application needing a separate polling relay process.
accepted_answers: CDC tools (such as Debezium) read a database's transaction/replication log directly and stream row changes as events, which can publish outbox table inserts to Kafka without the application needing a separate polling relay process.
hint: Read the database's own change log instead of writing a custom polling job.

front: Since the outbox relay delivers at-least-once, what must the eventual Kafka consumers of outbox-originated events still be?
back: Idempotent, because the relay can publish the same outbox event more than once (for example after a crash and retry before marking it published).
accepted_answers: Idempotent, because the relay can publish the same outbox event more than once (for example after a crash and retry before marking it published).
hint: The outbox pattern removes lost events, not duplicate events.

front: A consumer fails to process a message due to a transient downstream outage. What is the usual first-line strategy before giving up on the message entirely?
back: Retry with backoff, often by republishing the message to a dedicated retry topic (or delaying redelivery) a bounded number of times, rather than blocking the main partition or discarding the message immediately.
accepted_answers: Retry with backoff, often by republishing the message to a dedicated retry topic (or delaying redelivery) a bounded number of times, rather than blocking the main partition or discarding the message immediately.
hint: Give transient failures a few bounded chances before treating them as permanent.

front: What is a dead-letter queue (DLQ) in a messaging pipeline?
back: A separate topic (or queue) where messages are routed after exhausting their retry attempts, so they stop blocking the main processing pipeline while remaining available for inspection or manual reprocessing.
accepted_answers: A separate topic (or queue) where messages are routed after exhausting their retry attempts, so they stop blocking the main processing pipeline while remaining available for inspection or manual reprocessing.
hint: It quarantines messages that could not be handled, instead of losing or blocking on them.

front: Why is a single consumer that retries a failing message forever, in place, dangerous for a partition's overall throughput?
back: Because processing within a partition is ordered, a stuck message blocks every message behind it in the same partition from being processed at all, so one bad message can stall an entire partition indefinitely.
accepted_answers: Because processing within a partition is ordered, a stuck message blocks every message behind it in the same partition from being processed at all, so one bad message can stall an entire partition indefinitely.
hint: Per-partition ordering means one poison message can wedge everything behind it.

front: Why should a DLQ message typically preserve the original message's metadata (topic, partition, offset, headers, error) rather than just the raw payload?
back: That metadata lets an on-call engineer or reprocessing tool understand why the message failed and where it came from, and safely replay it back to the original topic once the underlying issue is fixed.
accepted_answers: That metadata lets an on-call engineer or reprocessing tool understand why the message failed and where it came from, and safely replay it back to the original topic once the underlying issue is fixed.
hint: The payload alone doesn't explain the failure or how to recover from it.

front: Why does bumping max.poll.records too high on a slow consumer risk triggering unwanted rebalances?
back: If processing the fetched batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, the broker assumes the consumer has died and reassigns its partitions, even though the consumer was just still working through a large batch.
accepted_answers: If processing the fetched batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, the broker assumes the consumer has died and reassigns its partitions, even though the consumer was just still working through a large batch.
hint: The broker's liveness check is based on how often you call poll, not on how much work you're doing.

front: What is the difference between a Kafka topic using log compaction and one using time/size-based retention?
back: A compacted topic keeps only the latest value per key forever (deleting only superseded values for the same key), while a retention-based topic deletes entire old messages after a fixed time or size limit regardless of key.
accepted_answers: A compacted topic keeps only the latest value per key forever (deleting only superseded values for the same key), while a retention-based topic deletes entire old messages after a fixed time or size limit regardless of key.
hint: Compaction keeps "the latest state per key"; retention keeps "everything for N days."

front: Why would an outbox table's events be a good fit for a compacted Kafka topic keyed by entity ID, in some use cases?
back: If only the latest state of each entity matters to downstream consumers (not the full history of intermediate changes), compaction keeps storage bounded while guaranteeing the newest value per key is never lost.
accepted_answers: If only the latest state of each entity matters to downstream consumers (not the full history of intermediate changes), compaction keeps storage bounded while guaranteeing the newest value per key is never lost.
hint: Use compaction when consumers only care about "current state," not the full event history.
